clue.text: Changing the subject, that was a great fight (extremely late starting)

indicators.note: a word whose start is late has lost its opening letter, so the first letter is dropped

parts.note: an exclamation of admiration for a boxing contest: what a bout!

explanation.surface: A spectator gushes over a terrific fight that began late, while someone changes the subject.
explanation.walkthrough: WHAT A BOUT plus (v)ERY. Whataboutery is deflecting criticism by asking 'what about...?' some other matter.
explanation.definitionFit: Whataboutery is the debating tactic of deflecting an accusation by raising a different issue, so it changes the subject.

clue.text: Largely unable to bear Commoners?

indicators.note: largely means most but not all, so the final letter is cut off

parts.note: the organ needed to bear children
without, as a suffix: WOMB-LESS is unable to bear young

explanation.surface: Ordinary people, the commoners, are mostly unable to put up with something.
explanation.walkthrough: WOMBLESS, unable to bear children, loses its last letter. The Wombles are furry creatures from a British children's series who live on Wimbledon Common, hence 'Commoners'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Wombles are fictional residents of Wimbledon Common, so they are punningly Commoners; the question mark flags the wordplay sense.

clue.text: Rise for workers?

parts.note: surface reading: a pay rise for employees
setter's reading: a small mound of earth built by and for worker insects

explanation.walkthrough: 'Rise' looks like a pay increase; it is a hillock, and the workers are worker ants.
explanation.definitionFit: An anthill is a mound, a rise in the ground, built by colonies of worker ants as their nest.

clue.text: In most of country, English ultimately thought, 'Why this Tory policy?'

indicators.note: one element is placed inside the other, the country's shortened name
most of a word means all except its final letter
ultimately points to the final letters of the following words

explanation.surface: Someone mid-country wonders why the Conservatives pursue this policy.
explanation.walkthrough: E goes into AUSTRI(a), then the last letters of 'thought' and 'Why'. The clue's question doubles as the definition: this is the policy being asked about.
explanation.definitionFit: Austerity, deep cuts to public spending, was the defining economic policy of the Conservative government after 2010.

clue.text: Killers deeply sceptical at first, following men around

parts.note: other ranks, soldiers who are not officers

indicators.note: at first points to the opening letter of the word before it

parts.note: surface padding: it only colours the picture and supplies no letters

explanation.surface: Murderers are deeply doubtful at first while trailing some men.
explanation.walkthrough: 'following' puts the S after the other two pieces, and 'men' as other ranks is a crossword staple. Killer whale is another name for the orca.
explanation.definitionFit: Orcas are popularly called killer whales, so killers is a shortened nickname for them.

clue.text: Dangerous wind; might its outcome be 'concerning'?

definitions.meaning: second meaning, read cryptically: split as ..., an instruction whose result is RE, meaning concerning

explanation.walkthrough: The second half splits the answer into an instruction: twist the letters ER and you get RE, the crossword word for 'concerning' or 'about'.
explanation.definitionFit: A twister is American slang for a tornado, a violent and dangerous rotating windstorm.

clue.text: Green's naked — can't possibly perform again

indicators.note: naked means stripped of its covering, so the outer letters are removed
possibly suggests one of several arrangements of those letters
the word can't loses its apostrophe and is read as plain letters

parts.note: taken as written, minus the apostrophe

explanation.surface: A man named Green is unclothed and unable to perform again.
explanation.walkthrough: (g)REE(n) then a jumble of CANT.
explanation.definitionFit: To re-enact is to act something out once more, i.e. to perform it again.

clue.text: Ted meddling with dangerous plant

indicators.note: meddling interferes and disturbs things, so the letters are thrown out of order

explanation.surface: A man called Ted tampers with a hazardous plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Adder's-tongue is a small fern, named for its spike resembling a snake's tongue, so it is a kind of plant.

clue.text: Puts down protest — determined to make comeback

indicators.note: coming back means travelling the other way, so the word runs right to left

explanation.surface: Authorities crush a protest that is resolved to return.
explanation.definitionFit: To demote someone is to put them down to a lower rank or position.

clue.text: Fancy that's first bell?

parts.note: A is first, as in a grade or the alphabet

explanation.surface: An exclamation of surprise: fancy that, the first bell has rung!
explanation.walkthrough: Read as 'first bell' the way one says 'bell A': CHIMER labelled A. 'Fancy that' looks like a set phrase, but 'that's' is only the link.
explanation.definitionFit: A chimera is a wild fantasy or illusion, and fancy as a noun means an imagined notion.

clue.text: No compromise in Parliament (abandoned by Opposition leader)

indicators.note: the combined pieces go inside the assembly's name

parts.note: lorn is an old word for forsaken

indicators.note: a leader comes at the front, so only the initial letter of the word is kept

explanation.surface: Parliament, deserted by the leader of the Opposition, refuses any compromise.
explanation.walkthrough: The Althing is Iceland's parliament, one of the oldest in the world; 'abandoned by' means the O tags along after the word for abandoned, and the pair sits inside.
explanation.definitionFit: All or nothing describes a stance that accepts no middle ground: either everything or nothing at all.

clue.text: Point to butcher briefly close to bridge going round Serpentine

indicators.note: turning round means facing the opposite way, so the whole string is read backwards
briefly means cut short, so the last letter of that word goes

parts.note: a butcher of people is a killer

indicators.note: the close of a word is its final letter

explanation.surface: Someone points to a butcher near a bridge over the Serpentine, the lake in London's Hyde Park.
explanation.walkthrough: E + KILLE(r) + E, all turned back. The Serpentine looks like the Hyde Park lake but is an adjective here.
explanation.definitionFit: Serpentine means snaky, winding like a serpent, and an eel is a fish with a long snakelike body.

clue.text: Trouble to follow — bands start on the drink

explanation.surface: Trouble follows when musical bands begin drinking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the drink' is slang for the sea, not alcohol.
explanation.definitionFit: To set sail is to begin a voyage, and the drink is informal for the sea.

clue.text: Part of crust contains special fibre

indicators.note: contains means holds inside, so one element wraps around the other

parts.note: sial is the geologists' term for the upper layer of the Earth's continental crust
S is an abbreviation for special

explanation.surface: A piece of bread crust contains some special fibre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Part of crust' looks like a hidden-word signal; it is the rock layer SIAL, holding S.
explanation.definitionFit: Sisal is a strong natural fibre from an agave plant, used for rope and matting.

clue.text: He succeeds becoming hornier — it's fantastic!

indicators.note: fantastic suggests something wildly fanciful, so the letters are reworked freely

explanation.surface: A man boasts of success as he grows randier, calling it fantastic.
explanation.definitionFit: An inheritor is an heir, one who succeeds to an estate or title after the previous holder.

clue.text: One may be in bed, commando, under cover (reportedly)

indicators.note: reportedly means as heard said, so the words count by their sound

parts.note: a ranger is a commando soldier, and hide means stay under cover

explanation.surface: A commando hides in a bed under the covers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bed' is a flower bed, not a sleeping place.
explanation.definitionFit: A hydrangea is a flowering shrub commonly planted in garden beds.

clue.text: Heartless puzzle today unfortunately — comprehensively beaten

indicators.note: unfortunately suggests things have gone wrong, so the letters end up disordered
without a heart means the central letters are removed

explanation.surface: A solver admits that today's puzzle has thoroughly defeated them.
explanation.walkthrough: PUZZLE loses its middle ZZ to leave PULE, which is mixed with TODAY.
explanation.definitionFit: To be outplayed is to be thoroughly defeated by an opponent who performed better.

clue.text: Originally came here to get treatment for foot

indicators.note: a treatment works the material over, so the letters are rearranged
originally means at the origin, so only the opening letter is taken

explanation.surface: A patient came here to have their foot treated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'foot' looks medical; it is a unit of poetic metre.
explanation.definitionFit: A trochee is a metrical foot of one stressed syllable followed by an unstressed one.

clue.text: Joe is stopping nearby — it's only to be expected

indicators.note: something stopping a gap plugs it, so one element is lodged inside another

parts.note: GI Joe, slang for an American soldier

explanation.surface: A man called Joe is stopping in the neighbourhood, as you'd expect.
explanation.definitionFit: Something logical follows naturally from the circumstances, so it is only to be expected.

clue.text: In short, era itself deliberately old-fashioned

indicators.note: the answer itself means looking back, so the letters are read backwards
in means the letters sit inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters spanning the end of short and the start of era

explanation.surface: A short era is self-consciously behind the times.
explanation.walkthrough: The hidden letters run backwards; 'itself' is a sly hint that the answer, short for retrospective, means looking back.
explanation.definitionFit: Retro describes a style that deliberately imitates fashions of the past, so it is old-fashioned on purpose.

clue.text: Metal band's employee listening, I think

indicators.note: listening means taking in by ear, so the word is chosen by its sound

parts.note: a roadie handles a touring band's equipment
um is the noise of someone pausing to think

explanation.surface: A heavy metal band's roadie eavesdrops, unsure of himself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Metal' suggests heavy metal music; it is the chemical element.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhodium is a rare, silvery precious metal, a chemical element in the platinum group.

clue.text: Set off from Thailand by ship

parts.note: T is Thailand's international vehicle code
a rigger is a ship with a given rig, as in square-rigger

explanation.surface: A traveller departs from Thailand on a boat.
explanation.definitionFit: To trigger is to set off, as in setting off an alarm or a chain of events.

clue.text: State what's on my mind?

parts.note: surface reading: a request to say what you are thinking
setter's reading: 'State' is a noun, a US state, and the rest is the title of a famous Ray Charles song about it

explanation.walkthrough: 'State' looks like a verb meaning say; it is a noun, a US state that a famous song puts on the singer's mind.
explanation.definitionFit: Georgia is a US state, and the classic song 'Georgia on My Mind' places it in the singer's thoughts.

clue.text: Admit leaving College Green

indicators.note: leaving means departing, so that letter goes out of the word

parts.note: C is an abbreviation for college

explanation.surface: Someone is let in as they leave College Green.
explanation.walkthrough: College Green looks like a place name; the two words are separate parts of the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To allow someone in is to admit them, letting them enter.

clue.text: A throwback is hard to get rid of

indicators.note: back means going in the opposite direction, so that word is read right to left

parts.note: to lob is to throw; the back half of the word is the reversal signal
H is the pencil abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: A relic of the past is difficult to do away with.
explanation.walkthrough: 'throwback' looks like one word meaning a relic; it splits into throw and a reversal signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To abolish something is to do away with it formally, so to get rid of it.

clue.text: Hello, Charlie — visiting in retrospect dead right

indicators.note: a visitor is a guest within someone's home, so these letters go inside another word
in retrospect means looking backwards, so the word runs right to left

parts.note: Charlie is C in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Greeting Charlie on a visit, someone realises in hindsight they were absolutely correct.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dead right' looks like a phrase meaning exactly right; dead belongs to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Ethical means morally right, in keeping with principles of good conduct.

clue.text: Almost happening

explanation.definitionFit: Going on means approaching a number or age, and also means taking place at the moment.

clue.text: Bird or tool

parts.note: or is the heraldic word for gold or yellow

explanation.surface: A choice is offered between a bird and a tool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'or' looks like a mere conjunction; in heraldry it is the colour gold.
explanation.definitionFit: The yellowhammer is a small yellow-headed bunting, a common European bird.
